title: What a kidney stone is
text: A kidney stone is a solid deposit that develops from substances in urine. It may remain in a kidney or travel into the urinary tract. Stones vary in size, shape, composition and location; these differences affect symptoms and treatment. Renal calculus, nephrolithiasis and urolithiasis are related terms you may see in a report.

title: Stone type changes the prevention plan
text: The main stone groups are calcium stones, uric acid stones, infection-related struvite stones and cystine stones. Calcium stones include calcium oxalate and calcium phosphate. A prevention plan should use stone analysis and relevant urine or blood results, not just an image classifier output saying stone. Do not assume that all stones require the same diet or medicine.

title: Calcium oxalate stones
text: Calcium oxalate is a common stone composition. Having a calcium-containing stone does not mean you should remove normal food calcium from your diet. Adequate dietary calcium can bind oxalate in the digestive tract. Discuss food choices with a clinician or dietitian, especially if urine testing shows high oxalate or calcium.

title: Calcium phosphate stones
text: Calcium phosphate is another calcium-containing stone type. A clinician may investigate the reason for repeated stones and tailor prevention to laboratory findings. General advice includes avoiding excessive sodium and keeping appropriate food calcium. Advice intended for calcium oxalate stones should not automatically become a strict oxalate restriction for every calcium phosphate stone former.

title: Struvite and infection-related stones
text: Struvite stones are associated with some urinary infections and may grow quickly. Management needs assessment of both the stone and the infection. They are not simply a dietary problem. Fever, chills, significant flank pain or feeling very unwell with a suspected stone calls for urgent medical care rather than waiting for a diet change to work.

title: Cystine stones are not kidney cysts
text: Cystine stones arise from cystinuria, an inherited disorder that allows excess cystine into urine. They are solid stones, not fluid-filled kidney cysts. The similar spelling must not send a cystinuria question to the simple-cyst advice pathway. Prevention often needs ongoing specialist care and an individualized fluid and treatment plan.

title: Renal colic and the pattern of pain
text: A moving or obstructing stone may cause sharp pain in the back, side, lower abdomen or groin. Pain may come in waves and can change location. This pattern can suggest a stone but is not diagnostic; other conditions can cause similar pain. New severe pain should be assessed promptly rather than diagnosed by chat.

title: Vomiting and inability to keep fluids down
text: Nausea and vomiting can accompany stone pain. Repeated vomiting may lead to dehydration and can make it impossible to take prescribed medicines or maintain fluids. Seek urgent care if vomiting persists or you cannot keep fluids down. Severe dehydration may require hospital treatment; drinking larger amounts at home is not always sufficient.

title: Citrus drinks are not a cure
text: Some citrus drinks contain citrate, which may help reduce crystal formation in certain settings. They are not a universal stone-dissolving treatment and do not replace prescribed care.
